title: Debugging and sanitizing tools: address, undefined behaviour and memory diagnostics
learningObjectives: Distinguish compile-time diagnostics, debugger observations and runtime sanitizer reports.
Explain the classes of defects commonly detected by address and undefined-behaviour sanitizers on supported toolchains.
Build a diagnostic executable with debug information and suitable sanitizer instrumentation.
Interpret a sanitizer report using the first relevant stack trace and the invalid operation it identifies.
Design tests that execute normal, boundary, invalid and cleanup paths rather than relying on one successful run.
Explain why a clean sanitizer run is limited to executed paths and does not prove the absence of all defects or undefined behaviour.

understand.concept: Debuggers and runtime sanitizers help investigate program behaviour. AddressSanitizer can detect many memory errors such as out-of-bounds accesses and use-after-free on supported systems. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer instruments selected operations that may invoke undefined behaviour, such as certain invalid shifts or signed overflow. These tools report issues on paths that actually execute; they are not formal proofs.
understand.whyItMatters: C memory and object-lifetime errors can remain hidden during ordinary testing. Instrumented builds can expose defects earlier, provide stack traces and help developers create focused regression tests. Tool support and runtime behaviour vary by compiler and platform.
understand.analogy: A sanitizer is like a test-site alarm that monitors selected hazards while a particular exercise is being performed.
understand.analogyLimit: An alarm that stays silent during one exercise does not prove that every possible exercise is safe. Instrumentation covers only selected defect classes and executed paths.

explain.narrative:
Compile with debug information and the sanitizer options supported by the toolchain. A common GCC/Clang-style development command uses -g, -O1, -fsanitize=address,undefined and -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Run a representative test suite and preserve the complete diagnostic, including the first relevant stack trace. Rebuild and rerun after fixing the root cause.

AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer are not interchangeable. They detect different classes of problems and have platform/runtime constraints. A report can point to the invalid access while the original cause occurred earlier, so inspect object lifetime, bounds, ownership and arithmetic. Do not treat a sanitizer report as a substitute for a code review.

A clean run means only that no instrumented issue was detected on the paths exercised in that run. It does not cover unexecuted branches, every concurrency issue, every implementation-specific defect or every possible undefined behaviour. Combine tests, compiler diagnostics, static analysis, reasoning and sanitizers.

examples.title: A valid bounds-checked array access
examples.explanation: The program checks the index before accessing the array. The commented command requests address and undefined-behaviour instrumentation on supported GCC/Clang-like environments.

examples.title: Detect and reject signed addition overflow before it occurs
examples.explanation: The function checks against the implementation's int limits before evaluating the addition. It rejects a null output pointer and leaves the output unchanged on failure. Boundary tests should include INT_MAX plus one and INT_MIN minus one, without performing those overflowing expressions.

practise.guidedTask: Build a small array program with sanitizer instrumentation. Run tests for the first element, last valid element and rejected out-of-range index. Record which code paths were actually executed.
practise.independentTask: Create a test suite for a dynamically allocated array or linked list. Exercise allocation failure handling where practical, empty and single-element cases, boundary indices, repeated cleanup and invalid operations. Run under address and undefined-behaviour sanitizers and document toolchain limitations.
hints: Use debug information so stack traces are useful.
Read the first relevant invalid operation and inspect the object's lifetime and bounds.
Address and undefined-behaviour sanitizers detect different classes of defects.
Fix the cause rather than hiding or disabling the diagnostic.
Add a regression test for every reproduced defect.
A clean run is limited to the code paths and instrumentation exercised.

questions.prompt: What does AddressSanitizer commonly help detect?
options: Out-of-bounds memory accesses and use-after-free errors
Every logical requirement error
All race conditions on every platform
Incorrect user-interface colours
questions.answer: Out-of-bounds memory accesses and use-after-free errors
questions.explanation: AddressSanitizer instruments memory accesses to detect several classes of memory misuse.

questions.prompt: What is a key limitation of runtime sanitizers?
options: They only observe instrumented defect classes on executed paths
They prove every possible path is safe
They replace code review
They guarantee portability
questions.answer: They only observe instrumented defect classes on executed paths
questions.explanation: Unexecuted paths and unsupported defect classes are not ruled out by a clean run.

questions.prompt: Why compile with debug information when diagnosing a sanitizer report?
options: It helps produce useful source locations and stack traces
It automatically fixes invalid memory accesses
It removes the need for tests
It changes every pointer into a safe pointer
questions.answer: It helps produce useful source locations and stack traces
questions.explanation: Debug information helps map runtime diagnostics back to source locations.

questions.prompt: What should happen after reproducing a sanitizer failure?
options: Identify and fix the root cause, then rerun regression tests
Delete the failing input
Disable the sanitizer permanently
Assume the report is harmless
questions.answer: Identify and fix the root cause, then rerun regression tests
questions.explanation: A fix should address the underlying invalid operation and be verified by rerunning tests.

questions.prompt: Does a clean sanitizer run prove absence of undefined behaviour?
options: No, only instrumented operations on executed paths were checked
Yes, on all possible inputs
Yes, if the program printed output
Only for programs with fewer than ten functions
questions.answer: No, only instrumented operations on executed paths were checked
questions.explanation: Sanitizers are valuable evidence but cannot exhaustively prove correctness.
